utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you please call out the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis, Matthias Neuner, Kyle Wood and our case manager, Alma Imamovic, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues from the Prosecutor's office and to all in and around the courtroom. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, with Nicholas Robson, representing General Delic, with our legal assistants, Lana Deljkic and Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. I see the witness is not in court. I believe there is a housekeeping matter to be raised. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you. Your Honour, the Defence, on the 12th of March of this year, submitted a confidential submission regarding omissions of the Prosecutor to act in accordance with Rule 68 of the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. Seeing that it's confidential, would you like to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. I will explain now why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We submitted a motion in accordance with Rule 68 of the Rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: Sorry, but I cannot find --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find the French channel. Excuse me. I'm the one perhaps who is confused, but I can't find the French channel. Could you speak in French, please. I've found it. Thank you very much. Please excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had just started, but I will say it again. So on the 12th of March, 2008, we submitted a confidential motion regarding omissions of the Prosecutor to act in accordance with Rule 68 of the Rules on Procedure and Evidence, in respect of several categories of documents which we specified in that motion. Today, on the 14th of March, we have informed the Trial Chamber that we have resubmitted this document as a public document, with one confidential annex, annex H. These documents, in the view of the Defence, are crucial, especially one of the categories of the documents which we name "the Italian collection of documents," which the Italian police or judiciary had seized in the Islamic Cultural Institute in Milan and submitted most probably to the OTP. So far, we managed to just look at the documents cursorily, and right now I can claim with absolute certainty now that those documents throw a new light on this whole new case and that they are perhaps absolutely crucial for the Defence of General Delic. These and other matters from our brief were discussed briefly with our friends from the OTP, and on the basis of that conversation, I am afraid that the situation regarding the non-disclosure of documents is even more serious than we had originally thought when we drafted the submission. There have been some problems in the Prosecutor's office which I do not wish to comment on and about which the Prosecutor's office will probably inform you. Why am I stating this now? Your Honours, for the Defence this is a new and unexpected, very worrying and alarming situation. From how it looks to us now, the Defence will urgently have to sit down, and perhaps we will have to review and consider another line of defence in relation to these documents, and perhaps review our list of witnesses in the light of these documents, as well as the actual list of documents that we submitted to the Trial Chamber and our colleagues from the Prosecutor's office. As to what exactly we will do and which steps we will take, I am unable to specify at this point, because that depends on the contents of the documents, which we would like to have translated. Some of them are in Italian. A vast majority of the documents are in Arabic. We just looked at them cursorily in order to see. We paid an Arab translator just to tell us what the documents are about. But it seems that the Prosecution has some other mitigating materials, and, Your Honours, we would like to ask you at this point to instruct the Prosecutor to urgently, in the shortest possible amount of time, respond to our motion so that you could make your ruling, because as I say, again, the Defence might have to review its position in terms of the continuation of its case. I do not want to take up any more court time or my own time to bring out witnesses whose testimony, in the light of these documents, would be unnecessary, and perhaps we will have to locate some other witnesses urgently, once again in the light of the said documents. At this point, Your Honours, I can say that shortly before the beginning of this session, the person who is the Arab translator and is looking through the documents, I -- sent me information that among the documents, there are combat reports from 1994 and 1995 which were sent from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the detachment, to the institute in Milan. At this point in time, Your Honours, I would like to just say that I'm not going to bring the witness that we had planned for next Monday, for the simple reason that we are unable to prepare these documents, to have them translated. We are not able to translate them into English, and even less into B/C/S for the witness to be able to look at the documents and to try to see if the witness could comment on these documents. The same thing relates to General Cuskic, who was supposed to testify late this week. At this point, Your Honours, we are trying to really find the best solution and to see what we can do with this evidence, without prejudicing too much the proceedings. We have lost the possibility of showing these documents to numerous witnesses brought forward by the Prosecution, for which we are sure they could have commented on the documents. I now have to stop some of my own witnesses at this point. The witness we were planning for Monday, he has already left, unfortunately, but I think that no time will be lost. I will be able to have some sort of preliminary interview with him. And also Witness Cuskic, who was supposed to testify at the end of next week. So next week, Your Honours, from what I can see, we will be only able to hear one witness. I'm very sorry about this, but at this point there's nothing more that I can do. I tried to see if any other witnesses who are coming after that can perhaps come at the end of the week, but this was not possible, at least not from this category of witnesses who are not in the same situation as these two that I have mentioned. Your Honours, I hope that you and also my colleagues from the Prosecutor's office will understand this situation. As I said, we will also try to see how to deal with this problem. I'm not going to go into detail about that. We did write down certain things in the brief. All I can say, Your Honours, is that as the Defence, we have taken a series of steps to avoid a situation like this from happening. I would just like to say that in preparation for this trial, at each status conference, we initiated the question of disclosure of materials pursuant to Rule 68. I think, and I'm going to check, I think that I specifically requested all documents that had to do with the communication with the El Mudjahedin Detachment with foreign centres, including Sheikh Shaaban, and I really think that we are not in this situation through any fault of our own. Also, you know we have taken certain efforts. We tried to get to certain documents that the Italian authorities had in their possession. Your Honours, for months we tried to get to those documents, but the Italian government was exceptionally uncooperative in relation to the Defence. We don't know any reasons for that. I believe that they were even uncooperative following your ruling. I also believe, Your Honours, that they have much more material than the material that even the Prosecutor's office has, and we are going to ask, as soon as possible, for your further assistance in order to gain access to these materials. I apologise once again to the Trial Chamber because of these two witnesses, but the situation is what it is, and there was nothing else that I could do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Just for my own clarification, when did you receive the material which you have now handed over to the Arabic interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, Your Honour. Your Honour, I think it was the 3rd of March, the 3rd of March. We received it definitely after we submitted our list of witnesses and documents. What we were able to put on the list, we did put on the list, but it was untranslated. A large document that we were given by the Prosecutor was something that we put on the list without a translation. The third part or batch of those Italian materials was disclosed to us on the 26th of February, and of course, Your Honours, we had to locate -- it's very hard to find a translator for Arabic who also is able to translate into English and B/C/S. This is the same problem the Prosecutor was facing. So this was the first time we saw this document, on the 26th of February. We immediately asked the translation service to translate that. However, as you know, they have particular problems of their own, and that's that. We were not able to resolve this matter. As soon as we found an Arabic translator and was able to give him the materials, he started to work on them, and he is submitting the information to me in batches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Madam Vidovic, if I understood you well, the purpose for telling us what you have told us this afternoon is: One, to ask the Prosecution to respond as quickly as possible to your motion compelling Rule 68 disclosure; two, to warn us that you are not calling your witness for Monday; three, to warn us that as a result of these disclosures, that the recently-received ones and possibly also the ones that are still coming, there may or there will be a change of strategy in the Defence case; and, four, you want the assistance of the Trial Chamber with respect to further information from the Italian government. Have I summarised your issues correctly? Okay, thank you so much. Mr. Mundis, are you --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to respond on the first point, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I think I can respond on the first point. Let me put one issue out at the outset, and that is: The Prosecution is well aware that the Defence has considered this type of material to be Rule 68. That is not an issue. I'm not going to stand here and say we were unaware that anything that falls into this category of material would not have been something that we would have considered to be Rule 68 in this case. And I say that for the simple reason that when we discovered that this material had not been disclosed to the Defence in mid-February, we took immediate steps to disclose it. As a result of that and as a result of the motion that was filed two days ago, we have undertaken a massive project in-house to determine exactly what has happened and what, if anything, still needs to be disclosed pursuant to Rule 68. I do not anticipate that I will be in a position to fully respond to that by, say, Monday or Tuesday of next week. I do understand and appreciate the urgency of the situation, and I can assure you that we are doing everything possible so that we are in a position not necessarily to simply respond to the Defence motion, but to provide not only the assurances that the Defence have requested in that motion, but to take it, in effect, a step further. Just to telegraph to the Chamber what it is we're doing, we have identified, through the assistance of an internal database that we have, every single document that has been seized in the course of this investigation. We are in the process of comparing that spreadsheet with the master disclosure log in this case and isolating out any material that has not been disclosed, and identifying whether or not any of that material falls within the scope of Rule 68. That is not something that can be done overnight. And once we have those results, they need to be reviewed on a document-by-document basis with a lawyer and a language assistant who reads the language of the documents. I would expect and I would hope that by the end of next week, that is, Thursday, since I'm aware Friday is a holiday, I would hope by the end of next week to be in a position to file a response, but I cannot at this point in time guarantee the Chamber that we will have undertaken the comprehensive review that we are undertaking by that point in time. I have redoubled our efforts with respect to any material that was obtained from the Islamic Cultural Institute in Milan or searches that were done, material that was seized, material that was gathered from the Italian authorities, and I believe -- we're double-checking, but I believe that all that material has, in fact, now been disclosed to the Defence. As I've said, Mr. President and Your Honours, I am aware of the Defence position with respect to this material. I am not in a position to explain why this particular group of material was not previously disclosed, and I have undertaken immediately a full review of all disclosure in this case to ensure that everything that the Defence team needs to put on their case is available to them. I do understand and appreciate, as you'll perhaps see from I believe it's annex D, this material that came from Milan was, in fact, put into the EDS, the Electronic Disclosure Suite. That is not sufficient. I fully accept that, as my letter indicates. This material was in Arabic. It was certainly not something that would have been searchable by the Defence. So with respect to that particular material, I will take full responsibility for the failure to disclose that. It was within our actual knowledge, and I accept that. What I'm trying to do at this point in time is to ensure that there's nothing else out there that needs to be disclosed to the Defence. And if there is, we will take immediate steps to disclose it. I think that's about all I can say at this point in time, pending this review. Obviously, if the Defence needs to recall any of the witnesses who've testified to cross-examine them on any of the documents, we would certainly not oppose that. I have indicated to the Defence if they want to amend their witness list or amend their exhibit list, we will not oppose that. With respect to any of this material that's now being disclosed, nor I would say we'll -- and I can engage my learned colleague from the Defence on this point in time. We would probably be amenable to any kind of Bar Table motion with respect to some of this material as well. So we will take whatever steps are necessary to ensure that the Defence is in a position to put forward the case that they think that they need to put forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Just a point of clarification for me. I hear you, in the same breath, talking about ability to respond and promising to respond by next Thursday, but also about acknowledging the fact that you were aware of material that is Rule 68 that is within your possession, that you will take immediate steps to disclose it. Given those two points all in one, do I understand you to be saying that you agree you do owe the Defence some Rule 68 material, and therefore you are going to disclose it, or are you saying, "No, no, no, I'm going to respond to your motion, and I'm going to respond by Thursday," or are you saying that the response will be also together with the disclosure to the extent possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me try to be clear. I understand what Your Honour is getting at. Our position is that what we need to do, in order to respond to the Defence motion, is to undertake an absolutely thorough review of what has been disclosed and to determine if there is anything else that needs to be disclosed. Once we are done with that review, we will immediately disclose anything that remains to be disclosed, and then immediately respond to the Defence motion, in terms of what she's asked for, what the Defence, Mrs. Vidovic and the Defence team have asked for is, at least as I'm reading it, an order from the Trial Chamber that we meet our Rule 68 obligations. What I'm saying is I need to determine if there are any outstanding Rule 68 obligations to be met, and then I can, in my response, report to the Trial Chamber what we have done in order to meet our Rule 68 obligations. To be as open and transparent as I possibly can, I'm well aware of what my Rule 68 obligations are. The issue, from where I'm standing, is: Have I met them or not? And I cannot respond to whether I've met them or not until I know if there is anything else that I need to disclose. And again, as I've stated at the outset, and I would hope that my learned colleagues from the Defence accept and understand this, I have -- this team has never taken the view that any of the material that relates to the material that was disclosed earlier coming from Milan is not within the scope of Rule 68, as the Defence perceives that. We are not saying, "We don't think this is Rule 68." We have always disclosed it as saying, in effect, "We understand you believe this is Rule 68. Therefore, we're giving it to you." So I cannot stress enough that we understand and accept the Defence position that this is Rule 68. That's not the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have identified -- we've found some material that should have been -- and I want to be clear about this. This material that was disclosed in February should have been disclosed to the Defence when we got it. I cannot explain why that did not happen, and I want to make sure that there's nothing else like that that similarly should have been disclosed earlier. And I can only give that assurance or take steps to immediately disclose it once I am confident that we have captured it all. And that's what's going to take me a few more days to complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Harhoff would like to know, when did you get this material that you disclosed on the 26th of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm looking again. I believe it's -- I don't know if Your Honours have the Defence filing in front of you. It's annex D. Annex D is a letter that was submitted by myself to the Defence team shortly -- what happened was this material -- we discovered that this material had not been disclosed. We immediately disclosed it. As a result, Mrs. Vidovic wrote me a letter, in effect saying, "Is there anything else like this? What else is there? We want it." And on the 29th of February, I responded to Mrs. Vidovic, and in that letter you'll find the dates. And what I wrote was that this material was registered in the Evidence Unit on the 3rd of March, 2006. It was obtained sometime after the 19th of January, 2006, and before the 3rd of March, 2006. In other words, we have it at least since March 3, 2006. It was -- and as I also indicate in the letter, it was put into EDS on the 18th of May, but I do -- 18th of May, 2006, but I do fully appreciate that because large amounts of this material were in Arabic, it would not have turned up in an electronic search of this material. I fully concede that point. So as I've said in the letter, this material should have been disclosed to the Defence pursuant to Rule 68. That is a position that I am taking today. It should have been disclosed, and I am, of course, disappointed that it wasn't. But that's the point we're at now. We are trying to take immediate remedial actions, and I will report back to the Chamber, in terms of a filing and response to the Defence motion, as soon as I am in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Just one last point. I've forgotten it now. Oh, yes. Just for my own edification, in this -- and this is a general question, it's not specific to this problem. In this Tribunal, there is a disclosure of all material that the Prosecution intends using to prove its case, in terms of Rule 66. Then -- and that disclosure is compulsory. Then there is a compulsory disclosure, in terms of Rule 68, of all exculpatory material. Why don't you just turn everything that you have to the -- it looks like this disclosure calls on disclosing everything that you have to the opposite. Why don't you just give them everything, "From Day 1, you get them," in Arabic, in French, in Japanese, in every other language?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Part of the problem, Your Honour, relates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except Rule 70 material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, that yeah, of course, and of course, perhaps witness-related material that deals with other cases, but if you're talking about giving them everything, there's two responses to that. First of all, define "everything," because if we actually mean everything, then they're -- we're talking about eight million pages of material, number 1. Number 2, in fact, excluding Rule 70 and excluding witness-related material, the Defence do have access to everything through the Electronic Disclosure Suite. So on the one hand, they have access to everything. On the other hand, to provide them with everything means eight million pages of paper, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it does seem as if you end up having to review eight million pages of paper in order to give them 7.000.999 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It might seem that way, and perhaps if I were sitting on the other side of the courtroom on the receiving end of all of this material, it very well might seem like I'm getting 7.999.912 pieces of paper. But let me, let me say that I believe that's why there's the specific requirement under Rule 68 that -- that talks about any actual knowledge of the Prosecutor, and that's a different kettle of fish altogether. And with respect to that actual knowledge prong, the material we're talking about today fits that perfectly, and again I want to stress that very clearly. But the short answer to the "make everything available to the Defence," the answer to that, of course, is the Electronic Disclosure Suite, in which event virtually all this material is available to the Defence. The problem then comes with particular subcomponents of the EDS, such as material in Arabic, material that is not easily searchable in an electronic format. So there are some difficulties, and of course when we provide Rule 66 disclosure, that's material relating to this case, we're not disclosing all -- or making available to all the Defence teams in the various cases, all the witness-related material, because quite frankly there could be need for protective measures or privacy concerns or other issues that relate to the witness-related material, but the document collection, excluding Rule 70 and excluding witness-related material is available in the Electronic Disclosure Suite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Madam Vidovic, you have heard what Mr. Mundis has to say on that point. Without elaborating, are you able to live with his response?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in principle, I am, except that I believe that my Colleague Mundis is aware, in this situation, as far as the material from the Italian authorities is concerned, that this was -- these were communications between the Chief Prosecutor and the Italian authorities. So this is a category of material that was not collected from different archives, where you're in a situation to receive hundreds of thousands of documents and you don't know what it's about. This is a situation where the Prosecutor's office knew that this was important material, they knew what it was about, and therefore they should have been careful to determine whether there were exculpatory materials within them. Of course, I am aware of the position of -- I understand the position of my Colleague Mundis, but at this point what I would want to know, Your Honours, is this: As Defence of my client, I want to know when exactly I will get this material, when it will be translated, because as you know, I only had two months to prepare my Defence -- for my Defence, and this is what I want to know at this point, because I cannot wait a full month now for them to check their archives because after that time I would still need some time to check those documents, and then again I will be in a situation where all the witnesses will have gone who could have witnessed -- testified about this, except if I'm given the opportunity to recall either their witnesses or my own. And this is why I've put this before the Chamber, because I'm trying to save whatever can be salvaged at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand your problems, Madam Vidovic. That's why I was asking you to -- just whether you can live with it without elaborating. I'm trying to save time. Judge Harhoff has something to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber understands, Madam Vidovic, your situation, and I think you have put it as succinctly as you possibly can. Mr. Mundis, I think, has also put his side quite clearly and concisely. Obviously, the Chamber is going to do everything in its power, like Mr. Mundis has promised, to accommodate the Defence in its difficulties. We understand that the problem is not of your own making, and therefore we should give the accused an opportunity to prepare his defence. We understand that. Okay. All I wanted to find out from you, and I know you've raised a specific question, you want a specific answer from the Prosecution, when can you expect documents. Are you able to say -- to give that in one word?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, I'm not, because I need to -- I need to, first of all, reduce the preliminary list of all the material seized to what has not been disclosed. That material then needs to be reviewed. I will say, based on the preliminary cut that we made yesterday, that the overwhelming bulk of the material that was seized for the investigation against this accused is not Rule 68 material, because it relates to non-Mujahedin crimes for other crime basis for which the accused was under investigation, in a nutshell. So the initial response is there's a huge amount of material, but when you actually start looking at that material, it is neither relevant nor exculpatory with respect to this case. So it's not -- I don't believe it's going to be a large number of documents, but I don't want to say anything else about how long it will take us until we get a little bit farther down the track, in terms of seeing what we're actually talking about. I'm not talking about something that's going to take me four weeks, but I'm not also talking about something that can be done by tomorrow morning or by Monday morning. It's most likely towards the middle to end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the answer I think -- Madam Vidovic, that last sentence is the answer you were asking for. Given that, I would like us, if there is nothing else to raise on this point, to move to point number 2, and I would imagine that point number 2 is going to be impacted upon by what we have been talking about now. And point number 2 related to you, the Defence, not being able to call a witness for Monday. Now, given the previous discussion, it may very well be that it's not just the witness for Monday, but the witness for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday that you're not able to call. What are you saying on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this will affect the witness who was supposed to testify on Monday. The witness scheduled for Wednesday -- the witness scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday we expect will be able to testify. He does not fall in this category. And the witness that was supposed to be the last witness next week -- or, rather, the witness who was not scheduled for next week, but the week after, and we'll see what we can do about that and how to resolve that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me give you this assurance from the Chamber's side. Whatever difficulties you encounter as a result of this situation, the Chamber will try to accommodate you to the extent possible. Okay? So as it unfolds, you'll let us know what witness you're able to call and what witness you're not able to call. But just to get it clear, with respect then to Monday next week -- is it Monday or Tuesday? Monday. With respect to Monday's witness, are you then asking for a postponement for that day? We can record that we will not be sitting on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. So Monday and Tuesday, that and the next one. Can I just consult with my assistant, please. Your Honour, my assistant is pointing out the following: It is possible that this witness, who will start testifying today, so we do have a witness -- we have a witness who will finish testifying today, and then we have a new one lined up who is supposed to begin his testimony. It is possible that he will continue his testimony on Monday, so that is possible. So, please, let's wait for the decision about the adjournment for Monday. So, in other words, the witness who is coming after -- following the witness who is already here, he is the one who will not be able to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. So we will decide to what date we postpone as this afternoon progresses. I would imagine that -- for the sake of brevity, I just want us to wrap up points 3 and 4 in one. Point 3 is the change of strategy because of the information that is coming, and point 4 was the assistance that you were asking from -- that you may ask from the Chamber with respect to the Italian officials. Can I wrap those two up by saying -- yes, ma'am, as we say, we will accommodate the Defence. The Chamber, to the extent possible, it will accommodate you on those two points as well. Is that okay? Fine. Does that wrap the discussion?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just -- I just felt that I need to respond to one point that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- that was actually related back to point 1, something that Mrs. Vidovic said that I really believe needs to be responded to. This is on page 16, lines 15 through 25. I want to make it very clear, so that there is absolutely no confusion about this point, when Mrs. Vidovic said, at line 22 through 25 of page 16: "This is a situation where the Prosecutor's office knew that this was important, knew what it was about, and therefore should have been careful to determine whether there was exculpatory materials within them," I want to be absolutely 100 per cent transparent here that this was an error on the part of the Prosecution. It's not a question of we should have known. It's a question of we did know, and in this respect, with respect to this material, the buck stops right here as the responsible party. So I want to be absolutely clear on that, and I want the Defence to fully understand the importance of what we're talking about here and the seriousness with which this team takes that obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you had said so earlier, Mr. Mundis. We understood you, and I'm sure that Madam Vidovic takes that on board. Thank you very much for, in the case, stressing that point once again. I guess this wraps up the issue. If we -- I don't know -- shall we call the witness or do you want us to rule on yesterday's objection in his absence? It arose in his presence. Madam Vidovic, I think you should be the dominus litis on this one, and we should defer to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps it is better for you to give your ruling without the witness being present. I think it's always better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The Trial Chamber finds itself in a situation where it cannot rule on this objection for the reasons I'm just about to give. 1. Madam Vidovic, you said yesterday: "But he will have an opportunity to answer in detail on this issue, Mr. Neuner, and it's very probable that we will address the Judges panel on this issue in a while, and he will have the opportunity to address it then." As a result of that statement, Mr. Mundis stood up and said: "Before the Chamber renders a decision, I would simply telegraph that Mrs. Vidovic has discussed this issue with me." Now, it looks like the Trial Chamber is being called upon to make a ruling on this objection based, amongst others, on a discussion that took place to which this Trial Chamber is not privy, a discussion that took place somewhere else. Now, on the basis of what is before the -- and let me be very clear. I am not suggesting that the parties must tell us what they discussed, because it may be something that you don't want the Trial Chamber to know. But on the basis of what was before us yesterday, we find it difficult to uphold this objection, but we also appreciate that it looks like there may be something here that is important and that at a later stage, if this matter is not resolved now, may lengthen the proceedings. Now, we don't want to lengthen the proceedings. We would like to exercise our discretion in a way that makes the proceedings expeditious and we therefore wanted to find out from both sides whether you are able to motivate your positions a little more. You don't have to tell us what is not -- what we are not supposed to hear, but give us a good reason to be able to make a ruling here, particularly because, Madam Vidovic, you said, where I quoted you, that you will address us on this issue in a while. Now, it looks we've got the cart before the horse here. We're now being asked to make a ruling before we are addressed. So this is the difficulty we're finding ourselves in.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. Your Honour, this has to do with an issue that relates to the contact of the Office of the Prosecution with our witnesses. I don't mean the Office of the Prosecutor, but some individuals from the Office of the Prosecutor. And I've discussed this with my colleague, Mr. Mundis. Your Honour, at this point -- I don't think at this point it would take too much -- it would be too wide a scope, and I don't think I want to broach this topic now, or, rather, I think this is an issue that should be further discussed between me and Mr. Mundis and that we should try and resolve some of these problems in these discussions. It seems to me that Mr. Mundis has a lot of understanding for some of the proposals and some of the suggestions that I made in that respect. Now, I don't think that this issue may affect the length of the proceedings, themselves. In this situation, what kind of affect it can have on the situation we had yesterday at the end of the day, let me try and put this into a legal framework. Both sides in these proceedings and the Trial Chamber will find themselves in this situation, this legal framework: The colleague who was questioning the witness and did the cross-examination, then I had some re-examination and asked some questions, and my main concern -- my main objection had to do with this, that this was not -- that he was not questioning about something that was arising from the questions of the Trial Chamber and that that was why the Trial Chamber should not allow him to put those questions. That was the basis of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that that was the basis of your objection. In fact, your opposition to his application, he realised if he asked those questions, he would be asking questions that do not arise from the Trial Chamber's questions, but questions that arise from your re-examination. Hence, he made an application to be allowed to put those questions. Now -- and this is what I was trying to cut this discussion short when I didn't go back to that history. Now, you opposed that, and in your opposition to that, that's when you mentioned that you will address the panel of Judges on that issue. Now, it seems as if you still do have a complaint about this issue. You will raise it, and the point where I'm saying we don't want to lengthen the proceedings is that Mr. Mundis rose up to say, "While this witness is here, could we please be allowed to ask him questions on this particular issue that was raised by Madam Vidovic to avoid possibly having to call him back or possibly having to get another witness to come and testify on those issues?" And that is where there is a possibility of lengthening the proceedings. And we feel that if we allow them to ask those questions, we will shorten the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if that is your view, then I will withdraw my objection. If you believe that there is that danger, then I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Understand, Madam Vidovic, when I started this topic today, I said we are not in a position to rule, but then I said, "However, we realise these possibilities." So this is what I'm trying to explain to you. This is a possibility that we realise, and we do think that -- mind you, we are groping in the dark, we don't know what is the underlying thing, except that what you asked the witness, and he told us that he was working from 2.00 and then goes straight to an interview, then go back to work, then come back for an interview. There was mention of four days, there was mention of seventeen days. We are aware of -- that's all we know, and we don't know what the Defence intends doing about that. We don't know whether the Defence wants to address the Chamber about that. And we've been asked to make this ruling in the air. So if we make the ruling, we'll be making it on gut feel, rather than on facts. And, really, the gut feel here is expeditiousness. And we would like, therefore, if we make that ruling, at least to make it with hopefully the consent of both parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a question that has not been explored enough by the Defence. This is the question of having access to witnesses in general in this case. We still have not explored it enough. And I've discussed this with my colleague, Mr. Mundis. I will speak with him some more. I'm not someone who would rush with a submission without establishing the facts properly first. Having heard your opinion, I believe that perhaps it would be advisable to allow the cross-examination or to grant the request from the Prosecution and then allow me also then to put some questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. May we call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We apologise to call you just for 10 minutes before we take the break, but we had to deal with other business that didn't need you. Mr. Husic, I need not remind you, but again I remind you. You are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony, to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your application is granted, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have a few questions relating to the statement from last week, and I can ensure you right away I'm only asking about the formal taking of the statement, not about its content itself. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we have, for a second, the statement on our screens. This is PT6254.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: While this is being displayed, you will remember that last Tuesday, you came to the Sarajevo field office, Tuesday of last week?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And this is the 4th of March, as we can see here on the lower part of the statement?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: For Your Honours, the dates in the English statement have not fully been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We see here three dates on the B/C/S version which you signed, the 4th, the 5th, and the 7th of March. Is it correct that on these three days, you came to the Sarajevo field office?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but also on Thursday I brought materials that I was supposed to look at and go through and correct previously. I brought those materials and gave them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will come to that. Yeah, I will just do it step by step. So the 4th of March, 2008, was the Tuesday; right?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And on the 5th of March, Wednesday, you also came to the Sarajevo field office?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: As well as on Friday, the 7th of March?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And have I a correct recollection that on Tuesday, the 4th of March, you arrived at about 2.30 in the afternoon in the Sarajevo field office?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And once you arrived, a general introduction was given to you; you were informed about your rights as a witness and your obligations?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I informed you that I was coming from my place of work after my work hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Correct. And in the course of the afternoon, three breaks were undertaken; correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But you remember that we informed you that the translator, himself, needed to have breaks because he cannot translate for such a long time; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in these breaks, upon your request and wish expressed, we also served you with coffee?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the interview that day completed at around 7.00 in the evening, is it?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And afterwards, we tried to drive you home, but de facto we couldn't do that and we organised that you came home by a taxi?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So I'm coming now to Wednesday, the 5th of March. You, as far as I can recall, came at 2.20 in the afternoon to the field office.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, also after my office hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And, again, breaks were made in the course of the afternoon, and coffee, if and when requested, was provided?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And this time, the interview concluded a little bit earlier at 6.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And on that occasion, you were handed out the translation of the first part of your statement you had given on Tuesday, this time in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and this is where the problems began, because the translation was very incorrect and my corrections were very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I come to your corrections. So that evening, we drove you home?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the next day, Thursday, you were not coming to the Sarajevo field office at all?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't come to the field office, but I was obliged, in the break between my work and the afternoon meeting I had at the school, to give the material to Mr. Mueller [as interpreted], who had come to get that material. But I had work all day, obligations all day at my place of work, at the school where I am employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Correct, but weren't you asked the day before when you wanted to have a meeting, and you proposed that particular time period, and you even proposed the place where somebody drove to in order to make the break from your obligations as short as possible?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that day I had too many things to do at the school and it was hard to find 20 minutes' time to hand that over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In fact, somebody drove to the city centre of Sarajevo, where you were probably working or whatever, and handed out of the car just the newly-translated second part of this statement in the Bosnian language, and in return he became your corrected version of the Bosnian language statement which you had received the previous day. So it was a meeting of about one minute; right?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it didn't last that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So apart from that one-minute meeting, you weren't obliged by the Prosecution to come to the field office that day or to undertake some other way; you had the time available to plan for your own business?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did need time to get to that place and to return, so it was some 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But you proposed it. You told us we should come there, and we accepted that right away, did we?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So I want to move on to Friday. On Friday, you came at 2.30 to the Sarajevo field office, did you?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And that day, in essence, there was no new statement taken or no further questioning done; it was just incorporating the suggestions which you had, corrections you wanted to have?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That and, along with that, a conversation about the map that we spent a long time discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have to say I, myself, was not present, so I don't know. But in essence, you had the opportunity to make corrections that day, is it, to the entire statement in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but on that day we spent more time on the video footage, maps, and then after that we did the corrections of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. So I have here that you left the field office at around 5.00, is that correct, on Friday?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So I have here you arrived at 2.30 and left at 5.00. This would then mean that you had been at the Sarajevo field office for two and a half hours on Friday?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sarajevo office is very far from my place of work. It was Friday, it was crowded, so I spent a lot of time on the trip there and back. I mean, every day it's crowded, but particularly on Friday it's very crowded in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you for the way going there or coming back. I was asking: The actual time you spent on Friday was about two and a half hours at the Sarajevo field office?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, are you still going to be a little longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm practically done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you had the opportunity to read your entire statement in the Bosnian language on Friday again?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you read it before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would this be then a convenient time to take the break? We'll come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has just been advised by the Registrar that the witness says he would like to make a comment at this point in time. Mr. Husic, what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I stated an oath and committed myself to saying the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, testifying practically for the eighth day over these past two weeks. I have understood that -- I think that two details are not quite clear and that they bring in confusion about the entire testimony. The first detail that I would like to explain is the problem of units in the Bila Valley. The Bila Valley is a territory, the population of which was divided or was joined on to seven units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of them were in the 306th, a part in the 312th, some in 314th, then some in 325th, then the 307th Muslim unit and the 17th Krajina unit. Besides these large units, we saw that there were also groups that were paramilitary groups. When they were at their homes, if an incident took place in a location anywhere in the Bila Valley, automatically a large number of units were involved in that incident, members from three, four, five, sometimes even six units, and this is what was creating confusion in the understanding of the situation in Bila throughout the testimony. The 306th Mountain Brigade, when there was an incident in a location, had its members, but in the same location, perhaps on rest, there would also be members of some other units. The other problem that I would like to talk about briefly, in a few sentences, and which also creates confusion in the whole of the testimony, and which I think was caused by the fact that the positions of the Prosecutor or the evidence is the dates that are stated erroneously there, because when we're talking about the June, the early June, the beginning of the conflict, practically, as of the 28th of May, the conflicts broke out. The complete valley -- entire valley was blocked, and for the next two days all the dominant features in the Bila Valley and around it were taken by the HVO artillery. And in that way, movement was prevented. Secondly, there was contact with the Chetniks at that time, and we knew that, and this gave rise to additional concern. Then on the 2nd of May, the HVO Army, in four neighbouring Bosniak settlements, issued an ultimatum for them to give up their weapons. Velika Bukovica, Bandol, Ricice and Radonjici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, the transcript says "2nd of May." Do you mean 2nd of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2nd of June, yes, I apologise. I'm sorry, I am sorry. Excuse me, please. So the 2nd of June, an ultimatum was issued to four neighbouring Bosniak villages to hand over their weapons, and when they did not do so, the HVO forces attack started on those four villages, Ricice, hand over their weapons after the attack, and they were moved out. Bandol was destroyed, it was razed. The homes were destroyed. Four people were killed. The rest of the population fled. A boy was killed who, when he was alive, was bound with wire, and he was dragged along the ground in front of his house. The population of Velika Bukovica, which was also attacked, fought until they ran out of ammunition. Of 30 houses that were there, only two were left from which they put up resistance when they ran out of ammunition. 18 armed people pulled out. They left their families to the mercy of the HVO forces, and actually, I think this is a key detail, those 18 people who pulled out of the area actually brought out the news about what was going on in this part of the Bila Valley. And you will understand that in all of these villages, the population was related in families or in-laws. After that event in Bukovica, the counter-attack was launched that is discussed here all the time. So when we're talking about an attack and when we fix that on the 8th of June, and you rule out the days before that, then you cannot understand that this was actually a counter-attack in response to an attack that was previously carried out from the other side of the Bila Valley. So I'm in a position that after eight days of testimony, I have to return, and if you understand me, psychological it's very difficult. All of this happened 15 or 16 years ago. I have to go back to my environment and live with people whose names and roles I talked about here. And I wanted to say this so that I would actually meet my obligation to fully speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Husic, for those words. Thank you. I don't think I need to comment on those words. Thank you so much. We appreciate that you have given us that bit of information. Madam Vidovic, do you wish to re-examine the witness on the modalities of taking the statement and not on what he has just told us now?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I wanted to put a few questions about the modalities of taking statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, the Prosecutor put some questions to you about the schedule of your interviews; when you went, how long you were there, when did you leave, whether you had coffee or not and so on. I would like you to say, before this Trial Chamber, please, how this testimony looked. Let me just cut things short. You mentioned that you had to make corrections to the statement. Why did you make these corrections?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I obliged myself by signing it, but I must say that each time, I would come after working for a whole day and after having different duties throughout the day. I emphasised that each day, I was tired, and I think that it would have been all right for the Prosecutor also to mention that, because I mentioned that each time. Secondly, what was the biggest problem in those statements, besides the fact that I was so busy, was the inaccurate translation or interpretation that I received, and I was tired -- well, I started, so if the Prosecutor wants to be quite clear about it, he could say what the first pages of my corrections looked like. There were a lot of corrections. Then I saw that this took a lot of time. I was working all day, and then I had to do this in the evening. So then I just simply focused my corrections on the most essential, necessary things. The way it looked was how after working for a full day, you come to an office where people take turns in asking you about events from 15 years ago, so that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, did you provide a clear statement and were you speaking in your own words?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What my objection or remark is about this statement, and what is frustrating to me, is that there are no questions there that were put to me. They are not in the statement, and my answer is being placed in the context of different questions that are being put here. And this is why my answer, then, seems different.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, who was there when you were giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecutor who is asking me here and Mr. Koehler.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Koehler?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Koehler.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this. Was that your first meeting with Mr. Koehler?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we met when I testified in the first case, in the Hadzihasanovic-Kubura case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that testimony, you also appeared as a Defence witness, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you have just told us that you spoke with Mr. Koehler. Just one moment, please. How would you describe that interview? Was that a professional interview? What was it like?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the way the interview with me was conducted, I refused to have any other contacts with Mr. Koehler. He knows that very well. I didn't want to come anymore, because those interviews -- it was still the time when I still didn't understand the position of a witness, and I was, myself, afraid. And in conversations, when I was still not sure if I should give a statement or not, he said to me that, amongst other things, that anyone who had spent four years in the war could be in the situation of having other people imagining what his role was. So I experienced that as a kind of threat, and this is why I refused further cooperation with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you told me this now, when you received a summons to speak with Mr. K oehler again?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I also wished to refuse to cooperate with that gentleman again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the answer I gave you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just wanted to object to the last question, though the answer was given. So far, the witness has not mentioned that he received a summons, but my learned colleague has just suggested that a summons was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I respond. The witness said that Mr. Koehler was sitting with him at the interview. Well, he didn't fall from the sky. He mentioned Mr. Koehler as conducting the interview together with him, together with Mr. Neuner, so he probably did receive a summons to go to the interview. That was the basis for my question. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I believe the answer my learned colleague has just given speaks for itself. "I believe that a summons was issued." This mere speculation, and it is put here to the witness in a leading form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Is it a material issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It may -- I also believe, in the context, if we talk about the behaviour of Mr. Koehler, it would maybe make a difference, whether Mr. Koeh ler is employing summonses in order to see witnesses or not, or also the fact, and that's my main issue here, that it is suggested in a leading form to witnesses, though we are in a re-examination at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, okay. Do I also understand you to be disputing that a summons was issued?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: For the interview last week, I'm disputing that a summons was issued to this witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you receive a summons to go and talk to Mr. Koehler, sir, or were you just asked to call at the offices of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was called by telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, at some point did you find out that Mr. Koehler was supposed to be among those to put questions to you?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I received this telephone call, I was told that -- I didn't remember all the details, but that I should come, and I recognised Koehler's name because I remembered that person from before, and that was the reason why I did not accept that until you called me when I complained or -- that I didn't wish to. And when you suggested that I should, nevertheless, go and respond to this call, then I went for the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Husic, thank you very much. This brings us to the end of your testimony. Let's take this opportunity to thank you very much for taking time from your very busy schedule to come and testify here in the Tribunal, and wish you a safe trip back home. I hope you have lots of time to rest when you do get home, before you go back to work. Have a good weekend. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. The Defence calls Witness Hajrudin Hubo to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Hajrudin Hubo," interpreter correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hubo. My make is Nicholas Robson, and I'll be asking you some questions today on behalf of General Rasim Delic. Could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I wish you all a good afternoon, everyone in the courtroom. My name is Hajrudin Hubo, born on October 4, 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I was born in the Mavrovici place, Visoko Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what do you do for a living now?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I'm currently the chief of the Verification Centre in the Joint Staff in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you hold any military rank?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Prior to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you have any military experience?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I finished the Military Academy, and I worked in the former Yugoslav People's Army in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I left the former Yugoslav People's Army at the end of August, sometime in September, 1991, in the circumstances of the breakdown of Yugoslavia and when the former [Realtime transcript read in error "four"] Yugoslav Republics of Slovenia and Croatia were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And following the start of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you take up any military duties at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Before the war, I was engaged in the Patriotic League, and by decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that everyone should be put under the command and control of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I reported to the Regional Staff in Zenica and joined, on the 6th of April, I joined the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, which year was it that you joined the Regional Staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Officially, on the 6th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, at line 15, I just want to record that I think I heard the witness say "when the former Yugoslav republics of Slovenia and Croatia were attacked," not "the fall."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think the court reporter would have caught that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when you joined the Territorial Defence, did you take up any position?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of the desk officers in the Regional Staff of the Territorial Defence of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you remain as a desk officer in the Territorial Defence or did your position change at any stage?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, after a while I became the assistant commander for intelligence in the Regional Staff of the Territorial Defence, and when the corps began to be established, I was the chief of staff, the Regional Staff of the Territorial Defence, in the phase when the army was undergoing reorganisation, until it was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to clear a few things, can you tell us, first of all, which corps you are talking about which began to be established?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, the reorganisation of the army was underway, and specifically this was the period when the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was being established. And the official date of its establishment was December 1st. Of course, it wasn't established overnight. It took some period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, again, just so we're clear, the official date of the establishment of the 3rd Corps was the 1st of December of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Concerning the position that you occupied, once the 3rd Corps was formed, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: When the 3rd Corps was established, as I mentioned earlier, I was also the acting chief of staff of the District TO Staff, because it was still in existence, the staffs of the Territorial Defence within municipalities were still in existence and operational during 1993 for a while. And when our staff was closed down, at the Corps Command, within its staff, an organ was formed that was called "the Organ for Spatial Structures." I was chief of that organ, and in fact I had similar duties that I performed in the District Staff under new circumstances and within this new organisation, which means that I still -- that it was still my duty to coordinate the activities of the territorial staffs, municipal territorial staffs, until they were closed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately when it was that you took up the position of chief of the organ for special structures within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: It is not "special structures" but "spatial structures" or "territorial structures." That's what's meant by "spatial." And this was approximately, if I can recall, in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand that the responsibility of the organ for spatial structures was to still coordinate the activities of the territorial staff, as you said, or did it have other responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Its primary goal was to coordinate the municipality staff -- the activities of the municipal staffs of Territorial Defence, because higher territorial staffs were subordinated to the Command, and there were, I believe, some 12 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, just to clarify something in your last answer, I don't know whether something was missed out of the translation, did you say that its primary goal was to coordinate the activities of the municipal staffs of Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, in one segment of the Command, and the municipality staffs were already logistically -- they had support -- were subordinated to the corps commands, but this was the phase when the staffs were restructured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you remain as the chief of the organ for spatial structures during 1993 or did your position change at some point?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I think that sometime in August/September 1993, there were some personnel changes in the Command of the 3rd Corps, and at this time I was -- I became the chief of the organ for personnel at the Command -- at the Corps Command. So this is -- this was called at the time "the assistant commander for personnel and replenishment."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, could you please again repeat the name -- the full name of the organ that you became the chief of?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The organ's name at this time was the Organ for Replenishments and Personnel for the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And did that organ's name change at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: In the structural changes and organisational changes that followed, this organ was later changed into the Organ for Organisation, Mobilisation and Personnel Affairs. But, in effect, it did the same duties, but there were only a different number of people employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I see. Could you tell us briefly what the duties were of the organ?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This organ primarily had the task -- it was a technical organ of the Corps Command, and its duties were organisation and replenishment of commands and units of the 3rd Corps, resolution of the status of the members of those units. In other words, it dealt with the structure and replenishment of units. This term "replenishment" can be clarified perhaps in English, but it just meant that the units had to be fully manned, as was -- as was recommended or prescribed by a certain book of rules for formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm going to come on to replenishment and what that entailed in a little while, but at this stage if I can ask you a different question. In August or September, when you became the chief of this organ, can you tell us, what was the situation like in the 3rd Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The situation was delicate in several senses. Specifically, in the organ where I was, when I arrived there, there were one or two other men who were, because of their dissatisfaction, perhaps, for the work of my -- of the person who was there before me, the records were almost nonexistent, and the situation, in short, was very, very bad, difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, if at all -- if you can, why the records were almost nonexistent? What records are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I'm talking about the records of personnel that belonged to certain units, and according to the organisational structure and formations within the Secretariats of those -- Secretariats that were under the law obliged to deal with replenishment, because there were many -- there were many irregularities in the work of those organs, so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last portion of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, could you just repeat the last part of your answer. You mentioned secretariats that were obliged to deal with replenishment, and there were many irregularities. Can you continue?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, I could speak further on this. I'm afraid it would take much longer to explain the situation in full, but it was the secretariats, under the law, had the responsibility, on the basis of the plans, the decisions of the Presidency, the laws and all documents, to carry out mobilisation and send personnel to man units. But this did not function properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to explain about the secretariats in due course, so we won't focus on that at this moment. Obviously, one of the duties of your organ was to deal with replenishment and the manning of units. When you took up your position in 1993, were the units of the 3rd Corps fully manned?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I said at one point most units, I would say up to 90 per cent of units, were not fully manned, either in terms of manpower or materiel. And I could also add another fact. In the beginning, we did not even have access to all this information so that we could perform analyses and take certain steps, so that we wasted time on this also to obtain that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in terms of the units of the 3rd Corps not being fully manned, was this a problem only during 1993? Can you tell us how long this problem lasted for?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This problem was, in fact, resolved, in part, when it comes to procedures and the carrying out of duties and roles of all of those who participated in the mobilisation of men, and I can say that up until the end of the war, it was not completely overcome, because of many different circumstances that could be described. For instance, there were many borderline municipalities that existed on different territories at the beginning of the war, and so on and so forth. There was a lack of documents and many other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could clarify something, Mr. Hubo. You said that this problem was not completely overcome. You said that this lasted until the end of when?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This lasted up until the end of the war. The official date was the 22nd of December, 1995, the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I want you to focus on is the issue of replenishment of units, the idea of manning -- of putting men into units. Could you tell us who or what was responsible for carrying out replenishment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The responsible organ was the Superior Secretariat for National Defence, and under the law this was the state organ that informed and sent people -- assigned people to commands of army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, for those of us that don't understand what the Superior Secretariat for National Defence is, can you briefly describe for us what that organisation is?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: It's not the Supreme Secretariat for National Defence. There were different levels.
