The Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in other words, was a ministry of the government. Below it in the organisational scheme, there were District Secretariats for National Defence that spread over territories of several municipalities, and each municipality had their own municipal organs, and they were all set up differently. Most of the work that had to do with replenishment and the manning of units was within the jurisdiction of the Municipal Secretariats. So in those areas where that was possible, of course, where I said it before, those that were not on the border -- from the border municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seem to have lost translation. I'm just wondering if it's me or the rest of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You and I are in the same boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Hubo? I think we got the last part of your sentence, but I'm going to ask you to clarify a few things. Just so I understand you, when we talk about responsibility for replenishment, that responsibility fell to the organs of the Ministry of Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Primarily, the organs of the Ministry of Defence, the responsibility was to conduct or to prepare the plans of manning, and the situation was such that some units did not fully abide by this. So this was a very complex administrative work that had to be done, but the primary responsibility for replenishment, mobilisation and demobilisation of personnel and materiel was on the Ministry of Defence at different levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. And just so I understand you, as to those levels, we had the Ministry of Defence at ministerial level. Below that, we had the District Secretariats for Defence, and then below that, at the municipality level, we had the Municipal Secretariat for Defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Very briefly, can you explain to us how, in fact, the Municipal Defence Secretariat actually carried out replenishment of units?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: First of all, the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence replenished the unit commands that were formed in the area of the territory of that municipality. They would be replenished on the basis of plans of replenishment which the units drew up and which were sent to the Secretariat for final execution. This is how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. So if the Municipal Defence Secretariat received a plan asking for units to be replenished with men, what would the Municipal Defence Secretariat do next so that men actually were sent to those units?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: If a unit were to be formed, its role was to choose the personnel from its records of conscripts, so the secretariats had records of all military conscripts from their municipal territory. On the basis of plans and requests, they would make the selection by age, by specialties and by need, and they would issue the summons and then send the soldiers, non-commissioned officers and officers to the unit that was being formed or that already was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You mentioned that the Municipal Defence Secretariat kept a record of conscripts. Can you explain this a little more about that? What sort of information was kept?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: In brief, each military conscript who, in the former Yugoslavia, served his compulsory military term of duty, would have all information on him maintained by the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence. So this data included the person's particulars, what they were trained for, the blood group, and a lot of other relevant information that was required so that the person could carry out any particular duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the Municipal Defence Secretariat kept a record of each person sent to a unit. Would the actual unit, itself, keep a record about the individuals coming to the unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: If a person, a military conscript, was included in this way, they would report to the unit. Then the unit would receive the so-called unit booklet or card with this information. So this card file was something that the unit needed to maintain on the particular military conscript in order to resolve any status issues relating to the person, until the time that he was no longer in the unit, until the point in time he was transferred, demobilised, or no longer in the unit for some other reason. The Secretariat in the municipality had the personal card with identical information, so those two cards and all the information on them should have been identical in the unit and in the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I see. So the unit card that was held by the unit itself, which part of the unit kept the card?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Each independent unit, the command of that unit, its personnel organ would maintain these records.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And was there any law or regulations that regulated this issue of keeping records about conscripts?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Records of military conscripts was something that we actually used according to the rules on the mobilisation of armed forces, which was taken over from the former Yugoslav People's Army. It was a kind of subsidiary rule, with all the relevant forms and details. And the legal basis on that was the decree on the criteria and norms on the deployment of citizens and material funds, which was published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of B and H 19/92.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you've just mentioned a decree on the criteria and norms on the development -- on the deployment of citizens and material funds. Your Honours, could we please bring up Defence document D547. Mr. Hubo, can you see the title of this document?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in the English version, I'll just read it out: "Decree on the criteria and standards for the assignment of citizens and material resources to the armed forces and for other defence needs." Is this the legislation that you mentioned that governed the issue of replenishment of units?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, this is the basic document pursuant to which all of these tasks were carried out, and which was binding on all of those who took part in the implementation of this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to refer to Article 42, which is at page 10 in the English version and page 8 in the B/C/S version. If I can just read out part of Article 42, it says: "The assignment of personnel to the army shall be carried out by the Municipal Secretariat which keeps military records of the personnel in question." Can you comment on this Article 42, Mr. Hubo? What, if anything, does it tell us?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, it says who was responsible for assigning and mobilising units to the army. There were also other subjects. There was the work duty, the police, civil protection, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you say it says who was responsible. This article confirms that it was the Municipal Defence Secretariat who had that role?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, that was in its exclusive jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can now look at Article 20 of this decree. Your Honours, this is at page 6 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S version. If we can just very quickly go to the page before this in English so we can just see that we are about to refer to Article 20. Your Honours, you'll see the heading's been chopped off. So we can see the heading: "Article 20." And if we can go to the next page in the English, please. What this says is: "During a state of war, army ranks may also be manned by military conscripts directly reporting to the war unit without having been called up by the responsible Municipal Secretariat." Now, my question, Mr. Hubo, is: You explained to us a procedure whereby the Municipal Defence Secretariat was responsible for writing to conscripts and assigning them to a particular unit. Can you tell us what the effect of Article 20 is?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Of course. This Article 20 says that in a state of war, the manning can be carried out in the manner that the conscripts directly reporting to the war unit without having been called up by the responsible Municipal Secretariat. I must say that in the initial stage of the war was the most frequent case. When we were carrying out an analysis, at least 60 per cent of the people had reported themselves, without any summons from the Secretariat, and joined the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could just clarify something in the transcript, Mr. Hubo. Did you say that in the initial stages of the war, this was the most frequent case?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I would say that the most frequent case -- as far as I know, only one brigade, out of twenty of them -- I don't want to guess now, but the mobilisation was carried out through the Secretariat. The bulk of other units were mobilised in this way, that the conscripts and those who were not conscripts joined the nearest staffs and unit commands with their own weapons, motor vehicles, and whatever they had that was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. This Article 20 was taken up from the law that ruled the former Yugoslavia, right, or is it something totally new, an article that was drafted for the purposes of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge, I really couldn't say whether this was something that was like that in the former Yugoslav People's Army. But according to me, it asserts the right of every man to defend himself or to defend his country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, do you know, if a man decided to go directly to a unit, was there any procedure that had to be followed?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This article enables a person to join a unit. The unit would usually assess if there was a need, if the person was trained, and so on. And then if it accepted the person into its ranks, and this later referred to the ranks of units that were primarily in combat areas and not in peaceful territory, the unit was supposed to draw up the information and again inform the Secretariat for National Defence with this information so that the organ could -- or the Secretariat could then update its records and continue to maintain them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the unit was supposed to draw up information. What sort of information should it have collected and passed on to the Municipal Secretariat for Defence?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: It was supposed to compile the particulars of a person, which is something that is provided for in this second part, and what was crucial was to record the date of engagement or the date of reporting to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: While we're discussing Article 20, I want to ask you about the next paragraph, the last sentence. And what this says is: "Army ranks may also be manned by volunteers in the manner envisaged in paragraph 1 of this Article." Can you briefly explain what this means?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes. This is part of the answer, and perhaps it's something that Her Honour, the Judge, would be interested in. This paragraph, it's referred to military conscripts, and military conscripts were people of 18 to 60, mostly men, who had undergone training. And this second paragraph says "including volunteers," meaning women, people above 65, or younger than 18, all those who are not included in this age category from 18 to 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So "volunteers "could mean women and men above or below military age. Did "volunteers" also include foreigners on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, the category of foreigners is also under the category of volunteers, because although they did fit into the age group that was required, they were not citizens, so -- and that was one of the conditions for them to be able to be military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you, sir, to be saying that people under the age of 18 could volunteer into the army and the army would accept them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this article practically permits that, and there were many instances of a young man of 17 joining up. They would lead horses, bring water, carry out some other duties. They were not assigned to the front line, but they did participate. This also applies to women. I can give you some information. I think that at one point there were 5.000 women in the corps itself. Nobody forced them to do that, but they simply carried out duties in logistics or communications, something women were able to do. In other words, they were all volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just staying with the under 18s, was there a cut-off age below which a volunteer would not be allowed? A 12 year-old, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Perhaps I wasn't clear. As for people under 18, these were just possible cases, and I saw that sometimes in the field, but the -- it was something that was a matter of the person. They had to go through training once they were 18, and then there were centres for training. After six months' initial training, these people were assigned and entered into the records, taking into account their youth and things they were assigned to lighter duties. It was out of the question to use children or anything like that. Perhaps you can find cases of young men of 16 or 17 who had come from a village and had come with their own horse who left, but they would be turned back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was the essence of my question. Obviously, we don't use children in the army, and I wanted to find out that if we allow children of under 18 to volunteer, was there somewhere where we say, "No, no, no, you are too young and we can't accept you, even if you volunteer"? You know, obviously you can't accept a three year-old but would you accept a 12 year-old or would you -- was there a cut-off age where you would say, "You are a child, you can't be allowed to join, even if you want to volunteer"? That's my question, and if there was such a cut-off age, I'm asking you, what was that age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say that in 99.9 per cent, we would refuse these things, they were not accepted. There were some cases of persons of 17. I did see some cases like that. But generally people like that were not considered or accepted into units, especially combat units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe you don't understand. My question is: At what age would you refuse to accept them? What was the cut-off age, if there was any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot reply to that question, because I don't know of any such cases. Once, I saw a young boy in the field who was leading his horse, and I asked him how old he was, and he said he was 17, but according to our records this was not possible, nor was it encouraged in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In this law, this decree, is there no such cut-off age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean Article 20?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, any article. Is there no article in this law which refers to that point that I'm raising?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was possible in the early stages, as I mentioned earlier, in the phase -- in 1993, recruitment centres -- mobilisation centres had already been established, and young men under the age of 18 were not mobilised. So the cut-off age was 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. In Bosnia-Herzegovina and in former Yugoslavia, how old do you have to be to enter the Military Academy? Was it 16?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was a student at the Military Academy, but I had -- before that, I had completed the Military High School. This was when I was 16, 17. This is Military High School, but you enrolled in the Military Academy after you have completed high school, meaning at 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but do you -- so you enter the Military High School at 16 or before 16?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA and afterwards, if it's the same law that was still applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was there a minimum age at which you could enter a military school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the former JNA, the minimum age was after the completion of the elementary school, which is boys of 15, 16. And in our case, the minimum age in Bosnia and Herzegovina for a boy to be recruited, there were no military schools then, was 18. I don't know if you could follow me and whether I understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, you told us that foreigners would fall within this category of volunteer. When you talk of foreigners, what sort of countries did people come from to join the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: In the category of foreigner, first of all, there were citizens of all the former republics of the former Yugoslavia who were not born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then of course also, outside of that, from everywhere around the world. So to stress it one more time, all the persons who were not born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, under this provision, they were considered foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And so far as the people from the former republics of the former Yugoslavia are concerned, which former republics did people come from to fight in the Bosnian Army, if you can say?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, I can say that there were people from all over the former Yugoslav republics. There were people who were born in one republic and they worked in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In other words, all those citizens who were born in other republics but were married or worked or were in any way connected to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I want to focus on for a moment is the procedure by which a volunteer could join the Bosnian Army, and I'd like to turn your attention to Article 46. And, Your Honours, this is at page 11 in the English version, and it's page 8 in the Bosnian version. If we can scroll down in the English, please, and also in the B/C/S. Okay, we're at the bottom there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Because this is cut off in the Bosnian version, I'm going to read it to you, Mr. Hubo. It says that: "The wartime assignments for volunteers shall be determined by the Municipal Secretariat, which shall first take statements from the volunteers to the effect that they wish to join the army of their own accord and then establish for such persons a central register and individual file cards as required for military conscripts. However, the word 'volunteer' shall be indicated on the card or a separate roster established for volunteers. "Volunteers shall personally sign the statements referred to in paragraph 1 of this article or leave a finger impression in case they are illiterate." It then goes on to say: "After completing the procedure prescribed in paragraph 2 of the article, volunteers shall be issued service and conduct books containing the wartime duty station assigned to them. The word 'volunteer' shall be clearly indicated in them." I've read the article out to us. Could you explain briefly what the procedure was, then, for a volunteer signing up with the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Let me ask it a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The article sets out the procedure, Mr. Hubo. Did it work in that fashion? Was the volunteer required to -- I suppose, to sign a statement indicating that they were joining the army of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This was in those cases where the Municipal Secretariat mobilised people who wanted to, who volunteered, and that that municipal organ had to do this. So these persons were considered by such secretariats as volunteers, and records were created where it was possible, in those cases where it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question. Do you know if volunteers from all over the world that you referred to made these statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I never saw that, and in my contacts with the secretariats, they never mentioned that anyone, any such person ever made such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps this is a convenient time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Absolutely. Can we come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hubo, before the break we looked at one of the ways by which a volunteer could join the Bosnian Army, and we looked at the procedure. In Article 46, at the end of the article it talked about a service and conduct booklet being issued. Could you tell the Tribunal, what was the service and conduct book?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Each conscript had a military booklet. That's a personal document, a sort of ID containing his data, personal data, including the blood type and the specialty, the time spent in a certain unit, and so on. So that kind of information would be entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. If at this stage we could please bring up Exhibit 785.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Robson, what would you like to do with D547?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, you'll see that I'm going to continue referring to a couple more extracts, but perhaps it could be entered into evidence as an exhibit at this stage. I will be referring to it again, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Only Articles 42, 20 and 46?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be moving around the document a bit, so perhaps if you prefer, we can leave the admission to a later stage. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to be dealing with quite a number of articles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll admit the document at this stage, then. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit number 1310. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 1310.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We were at 1215 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, 1310. Okay, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It was Exhibit 785 that I referred to. Your Honours, I apologise for the quality. For some reason it's been scanned in as a poor-quality document. I do have a better copy which I can pass around the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, you just talked about a military booklet and that it would contain certain information. The document that we can see on the screen in front of us, is that an example of such a document?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, this is an example of a military booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And so, for example, we can see here that it has information about the person's surname, first name, date and place of birth, et cetera, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where does it say that this is a volunteer, or does it say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just about to come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But before you get to that, what is the significance of that date, 18th March 1965? What is that date?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I think if we can move on in the next version ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, you've actually -- there was only one version of this document, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: One page each.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: One page each, yes. The purpose was just really so that you could see that there was a photograph there and certain information appeared within the document. I think Mr. Hubo's established that what we can see is a military booklet, it's an example, and what I'd like to ask Mr. Hubo is:

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The decree that we looked at talked about a military booklet being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you, but I'd asked a question. I didn't get an answer. I asked: Of what date is the 18th of March, 1965? What does it signify?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just see the earlier -- the earlier screen? I think that's where the date is shown. The booklet, if you take a look here at this booklet, you will see that it says that this man was born on May 20th, 1943, in Bosanska Dubica. That's on the left-hand side of the booklet copy. On the right-hand side, it says: "In military records since ... ," and then the date is from the year of 1965, but I cannot read the date. So this means that the man served in the army when he was 18 or 20 and that his record -- that there is a file record and that since then he is -- has been a military conscript. In other words, the Defence Secretariat is keeping records on his information from that date on. If he moved from a municipality to another municipality, then the information would be updated by that new -- by that new municipality. So this is the date when he served in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That answers the question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, we can see that this person was born in Dubica in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Does it follow that he was a Bosnian citizen?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, Bosanska Dubica is in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if the person had been born outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Article 46 of the decree talked about the booklet being stamped with the word "Volunteer." Do you know where that would have been stamped within the booklet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I thought the witness once said that that had never occurred, so how would the witness know where to put the stamp if there had never been an example of a foreigner signing up as a volunteer under this law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, did you ever see a military booklet issued to a volunteer or a booklet that had the word "Volunteer" stamped upon it?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I've never seen it, personally, such a military booklet, so that I can affirm here to the Judge that this gentleman, if he were, for instance, a volunteer from Croatia, where it says "Military record" there should be the word stamped "Volunteer" by this number, "3306261 ," because when it says that he's in the military records Municipality of Zenica, then there should be a word there affixed "Volunteer," and of course there should also be a file card issued by the Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robson, when you were searching through documentation, you never found a military booklet for volunteer; you don't have that available?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can confirm I don't have an example of a military booklet with the word "Volunteer" stamped on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, moving on, we just looked at the procedure whereby a volunteer would go to the Municipal Defence Secretariat and give a statement. I'd like to look at the other procedure that was envisaged -- or a situation that was envisaged in Article 20, where it was explained that the volunteer could go directly to a unit. In the situation where a volunteer went directly to a unit in the field, were there any procedural requirements that he had to -- or that had to be satisfied?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The unit would have had to compile a list of information that were required, as you can see in this booklet here, and such information should be forwarded to the Defence Secretariat so that they could confirm his membership and keep a record of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if we could go back to the decree, which is Exhibit 1310, and it's Article 48 that I'm interested in, which is at page number 12 in the English, and it's page 9 in the B/C/S version. Page 12 in the English, page 9 in the B/C/S. It's Article 48 we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, perhaps we can deal with this quickly. Does Article 48 confirm what you've just told us; in other words, that the -- a person within the unit to which the volunteer goes to had to take certain information and supply that information to the Municipal Defence Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, this confirms the procedure which you asked me about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can look at Article 51, which is connected to Article 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what Article 51 is all about? Perhaps if we can look at the next page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This article again shows when the Secretariat had received the list with the information from Article 48 and what they would have to do then. They would have to enter it into record, prepare documents for the persons from the list who have reported to a wartime unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would it also be foreseen that having taken that information from the list, entering it into the records, the Municipal Defence Secretariat would also issue a military booklet to the volunteer?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, that can be concluded on the basis of these previous actions, and it says here that the war assignment is written also in the record of those persons, meaning that the Secretariat would need to issue them the military booklets too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then just so we're clear, in the situation where a volunteer goes directly to a military unit, apart from the obligation of the military unit to send information to the Municipal Defence Secretariat, would there also be an obligation on the unit to keep information about the volunteer?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Of course, the unit was obliged to use all the previous information, update it, and maintain all the entries of all changes from the time when he joined the unit until that person left the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm going to come to the issue of foreigners in a moment, but before we do so I have one last issue to touch upon in connection with military booklets. Please, could we show the witness Exhibit 124. Your Honours, just to complicate things, I am going to be referring to Exhibit 124, but what's happened is that the Defence noticed a few words were missing from the English translation, and therefore what we've done is we've produced a new version of Exhibit 124 which is Defence document D1047. And what we're going to be doing is applying, in due course, to substitute Exhibit D1047 for Exhibit 124, so could we please bring up D1047, which is the same document as Exhibit 124 with the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What should we do now with Exhibit 124? At this stage, you have called for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it could be put away. If it could be substituted with D1047. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have your learned colleagues on the opposite side seen your corrected document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I can tell you is that the correction is in the first sentence of the first paragraph that we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, what we can see before us is a document from the chief of the security sector, Ramiz Dugalic, dated the 12th of September, 1993. And we can see that the document was received by the 7th Muslim Brigade. And in the first paragraph, what we can see is that it says that: "Through the operative work, we came to the information that a certain number of persons was using the military booklets as the identification documents and proof of the engagement within the RBiH Army, although they are not engaged and they are involved in other (even criminal) work." It then goes on to talk about the cause of such a situation is the lack of responsibility of the personnel bodies during the transformation of units. And then in the next sentence, it talks about that the information that shows also the fictive issuance of the documents as the cover of the engagement. Could you explain to us, does this document reflect the situation that existed in September 1993 in connection with military booklets?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, shouldn't you have led this witness on these facts first before you showed him this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an exhibit, and I was hoping to save some time by -- I'll certainly lay the foundation with Defence "D" documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But we want to know that this witness has independent knowledge of these facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw the question, and perhaps Mr. Hubo can just explain to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead, but I'm suggesting that at least in the future, talk about the issue first and then show him the document as confirmation of what he has said, rather than the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, are you able to comment on this first paragraph of the document that I've made reference to?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I can comment, but when you asked me at the beginning about the state, I found, once I assumed that duty, this is just one of those segments about which we talked. And this document of the security sector is practically trying in this way, along that line of command, to establish order or, rather, to organise all the necessary documents and all the -- respect all the establishment requirements. What is here associates possibly on the use of coercion or some consequences that can be drawn on the basis of this. I can add, not directly linked to this, that many people wore military uniforms without insignia, without documents, so it was a very difficult situation in terms of identification by uniform or on the basis of documents. So this is just one of those documents that intimates something like this. In this document, organs of the subordinate commands of the corps were supposed to place a stamp on a completed military booklet, once a person had left the unit. There was such cases, but a person had left and was stamped as leaving the brigade, when they were actually never a member of the brigade. And this is something that can be considered an abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, I'm told by my colleague that part of your answer wasn't captured. If you can please tell us about these persons that left the brigade and their military booklets were stamped as leaving the brigade. Can you explain, once again, what happened to such persons and what sort of problems may have been caused?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: There were a number of cases, and I can explain that on one example. You had the option, first of all, that a man voluntarily left a unit. Once he left the unit, the unit did not finalise his booklet. It should have stamped the booklet when he joined the unit, stamped his date, and when the person leaves the unit, they should also enter the date of departure and affirm that with a stamp in the military booklet. What would happen was that the person's date of entry would be entered, and the time of departure would not be entered, even though they had left of their own free will or because of some other reason. The person who would look at the booklet would then think that this was a member of the unit, although there was no legal basis for that. The unit simply did not maintain him on its records. That would be one of the possible cases of potential abuse. For the person who looked at the document, specifically for the military police, they were a member of the brigade, but formally, legally, the brigade did not consider that person to be its member as of the date that they had left the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what sort of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. In this situation that you're describing, where there's abuse and so on, could there also be the opposite? Could there also be volunteers who joined the army, but who had no booklet? As far as you know, all procedures were carefully followed and well followed, from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There could have been different kinds of abuses, and there were different types of abuses, but the consequences in that sense were borne by the commands of those units. What we are talking about here are specific individuals who abused this personal document. Somebody could have been considered to be something, but if this was not recorded in the Secretariat in the proper manner, then that would have primarily been that person's problem. They did not then get the status of a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From an official point of view, if they fought, as far as you know, do you know of cases where a volunteer that was not recorded and, according to this procedure, could have fought along with or within the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can give you an example. For example, the Municipality of Stari Vitez, Stari Grad, where the conscripts were also women, did they fight? They probably did, and they had weapons, but they were never recorded in the Secretariat. They were never given the status of army members. That a person could have had a rifle, could have worn a uniform, but if they were not registered in the Defence Secretariat or at the unit, they did not enjoy the status of -- that went with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, that's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, in your last answer, you said that if persons were not registered in the Defence Secretariat or at the unit, they did not enjoy the status of ... and then the transcript didn't capture the next part of your answer. What status did they not enjoy?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Specifically, it means that they did not enjoy the status of a member of the army, or a member of the police, or any other status that they would enjoy under the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask. I'm getting confused now, Mr. Hubo. Earlier, you told us that people out -- men outside the age of 18 and 60 and that women could volunteer. And when these people volunteered, they became part of the army, although they could be given jobs not necessarily on the front line. Now, in this answer, you are saying women conscripts were not recorded in the Secretariat, and you are saying these people who are not recorded in the Secretariat did not enjoy the benefits of the status of being members of the army. Is that how the women were treated in this army; they joined the army, but they never got the status of being members of the army? They volunteered into the army, but they never got the status of being in the army, so they never got these cards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I wasn't clear perhaps. It's like this: If a person was a volunteer in the specific case and they came to a unit, then according to the described procedure, the unit was obliged to draft a list with all the information and send that to the Secretariat for Defence. In that situation, that person would then have the status of a member of the army. If the person waged war by themselves and were not registered in the unit or in the Secretariat, there was no record of that person, then the person could not be granted such status. So those persons that were recorded in the unit or at the Secretariat for National Defence, they had the status of members of the army -- I'm talking about women -- because somebody affirmed that status. I don't know if I was clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know, either. I was just trying to understand the statement you made earlier, when you said: "Your Honour, I can give you an example. For example, the Municipality of Stari Vitez, Stari Grad, where the conscripts were also women, did they fight, they probably did, and they had weapons, but they were never recorded in the Secretariat. They were never given the status of army members. That person could have had a rifle, could have worn a uniform, but if they were not registered in the Defence Secretariat or at the unit, they did not enjoy the status of being army members." That is what confused me, and that's why I came back and said, "Are you saying women joined the army and women never enjoyed the status of the members of the army?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The women who were registered at the Secretariats for National Defence, that were in the records, they had that status. But those persons who were not registered as members of the army and did not belong to any unit, then they were never granted this status. And maybe it can sound like nonsense, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps these are not the easiest of concepts to grapple with at 20 past 6.00 on a Friday evening. But moving to a more concrete issue, Mr. Hubo, I'd like to ask you about foreign volunteers and specifically the El Mujahid Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina that you heard of the El Mudjahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, let me interrupt you, Mr. Robson, and I'm sorry to do so. Would you like D1047 to be tendered into evidence before you move on to the EMD?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we would like is we would like to substitute that for the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Is that what you would like done?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Have you seen the correction?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not a B/C/S speaker, but it seems apparent, on the face of it, that those words are missing. I'm satisfied -- the Prosecution is satisfied that the translation is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, then D1047 is admitted into evidence in substitution of Exhibit 124. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall be given the same number as the previous document, which is Exhibit number 00124. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, did there come a time when you heard of the El Mudjahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately the time period when you first heard of the detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This was in the second half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We've discussed the procedures for an individual volunteering to join the army. On the one hand, an individual could go directly to the Municipal Defence Secretariat and sign a statement, or, on the other hand, they could go directly to a unit, and then the unit would have to send information to the Municipal Defence Secretariat. As to the first situation, are you aware of any members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment ever going directly to a municipal defence secretariat and signing a statement?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: In contacts with defence secretariats, I never heard of anything, any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Concerning the second possibility of a foreign volunteer going directly to a unit, are you aware of -- are you aware of a situation where the El Mudjahedin Detachment ever sent the necessary information, such as name, date of birth, et cetera, to the Municipal Defence Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Information of that type were sent to the Corps Command in a certain period of time, and such information was sent -- I couldn't even call it "information," but bits and pieces of information that was not very easily discernible and understandable and incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. So information at some time was sent to the Corps Command, but my question was: Are you aware of the El Mudjahedin Detachment ever sending information directly to the Municipal Defence Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: As far as I was informed from the Secretariat, they never received such information as they requested. I could not really answer that question, except on the basis of what I had heard and the discussions that I had with my colleagues at the Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You told us earlier that the Municipal Defence Secretariat had an obligation to keep information in its records about each member of every military unit. Do you know if any municipal Defence Secretariat kept information about members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: They complained to us, in fact. They requested this from them. They complained, but they never had those -- that information, and that is why they turned to someone and tried to obtain it through some other channels, although it was the responsibility of the unit to report to the Secretariat directly and not through any other channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You told us earlier that each military unit had an obligation to keep a unit card containing information about its members. Do you know whether the El Mudjahedin Detachment kept a unit card containing such information about its members?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I don't know, nor was I ever in a position to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll come on to checking in a little while, if I may. I won't explore that with you just yet. A little earlier, you also said that the Municipal Defence Secretariat should have issued military booklets to volunteers joining the Bosnian Army. Do you know whether military booklets were ever issued to the members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I think the Secretariat never issued any booklets to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to bring up Defence document D969.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, first of all, can you see what the document says? Are you able to make it out on the screen?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Cannot. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This is an order from the army -- the Command of the 3rd Corps, sent to all units, of 18 July 1994, the purpose being to establish a single system of filing, as we discussed earlier, in the following -- in the items that follow. They describe the procedure and how this should be done in those municipalities that did not have their own territories, that they were temporarily in different -- in occupied territories, and it also points out in item 5 that all military conscripts that are transferred from one unit to another, that the same thing should be done; in other words, their card files should be closed. And in item 6, it says that units have the responsibility to inform the Defence Secretariat as soon as a new conscript arrives, and so on and so forth. So this is an order trying to establish unit card files, as envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So this is an order trying to establish unit card files. Just so we're clear, a unit card file, is that the information that would be kept within the unit or is it the information that's kept in the Municipal Defence Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Here, mention is made of unit card files, so these files had to be maintained within units, and they should keep these records. And it also says that these -- this information should correspond to the information that is held by the Secretariats for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at -- if we can scroll down in the English version, you say that the information should correspond to the information held by the secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In point number 7, does that specify the frequency with which the unit should correspond with the Defence Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The item says that the matching or the coordination of the unit cards should be carried out immediately with the authorised Defence Secretariats, and it also stresses that in the coming period, in the upcoming period, this collating should be carried out once a month. In other words, once a month, a representative from the unit and a representative -- should inform the representative from the Secretariat. They should compare their records, and the records that were in the Secretariat should be reflected and collated with the unit records, and they should be collated, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can look at the bottom of the document, if we can go to page 2 in the English version, was this document sent to the El Mudjahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, it was. This was also forwarded to all other units, because this was something that was topical up until the end of the war. This was something that related to military records.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you help us, do you know whether the El Mudjahedin Detachment complied with this order to immediately establish unit cards within the unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I was not in a position to verify that, but all the relevant persons from the Secretariat, and according to what we received from them, they never -- they never established such records. Simply, they did not have the information required in order to set up something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, you say : "According to what we received from them ..." And there you're referring to the Secretariat. You say: "... they never established such records." When you say "they," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I mean El Mujahedin, first, primarily. The other units, it was clear because we were able to verify these things. And as far as these units are concerned, I used the word "they" because you asked me whether they had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see that this order was sent to other subordinate units. Do you know whether the other subordinate -- well, these other subordinate units listed here complied with the order?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: We controlled the status by this segment of combat readiness, and this order was produced because the situation was such that it needed to be improved. So we had the opportunity to improve the situation, and it was improved on the spot. This situation was -- we continued to work on it up until the end of the war. It was never completely complied with, but we were seeking to reach that point. And you have to understand that at one point, this meant there were 70.000 people, and files should be complied on each and every one of these persons, and the secretariats very frequently, because of bad communications, lack of fuel and so on, were unable to comply with this in time..

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm just a little bit unclear about that last answer. I was asking you about other units within the 3rd Corps, and you mentioned, "we controlled the status." Could you explain that in a bit more detail? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question about the status? We tried to monitor the overall situation in this respect, not the status, because the status was something that was regulated by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a translation issue. What I can ask you is: Were you able to check whether other subordinate units within the 3rd Corps had produced unit cards for its members?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: We did this in all those instances where we had physical access. For instance, at one point in time Operative Group 7, Doboj South, was physically cut off from the Corps Command, so we were unable to physically contact them. In all other units, we were able to physically check the information, because we would send our people there and they would verify on the spot, check all the files, monitor, check how they are maintained, and so on and so forth, of course except with the El Mudjahedin Detachment, because we were never able to access them, members from the Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you say you were not able to access the El Mudjahedin Detachment. Can you please explain why your organ was not able to access the detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we didn't know who the responsible person was. There was a person who was sent as a courier with information when they needed it; in other words, whenever they felt like doing that. And, secondly, I, for instance, went on two occasions with a colleague of mine, and simply we were physically prevented from entering there. When you tried to reach someone by phone, you never knew whom to ask for or where to look for that person. It was impossible to maintain any normal communication that we had with other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll explore that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: When you say "we didn't know who the responsible person was," what would you have expected in a typical unit? Who would you have liaised with on these issues?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: In a typical unit, what I did was to try to get in touch with someone. It was usually one person. Actually, it was a man by the name Muris Supic there, who spoke Bosnian, who brought information when they felt it was necessary that it should be brought, insisting at least on a minimum, that person could not have been considered as a responsible person because he couldn't really say much. You couldn't rely on him as an expert and ask him for something and rely on his answer. He was just some kind of person who carried out different things and was a kind of intermediary because of the language and maybe because of his training. I mean, I don't know what else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm a little lost. I'm a bit lost, Mr. Robson. And, Witness, you said in your answer "in a typical unit." By that, I understand that in any type of unit, any unit, not a specific unit. But then when you said: "Actually, it was a man by the name Muris Supic there," I get the impression you're talking about a specific unit now, and I'm lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm told that the word "typical" was omitted and hence, the witness gathered -- I'm told --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to you and to my colleague. A part of the reply was omitted. In the first and the second part, the transcript did not catch the answer, and perhaps if my colleague can repeat the question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll go back to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, you started explaining to us about the El Mudjahedin Detachment. What I was trying to find out from you is: In relation to a regular unit of the 3rd Corps, let's call it a brigade, who would you have normally dealt with on issues relating to unit cards? Shall I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I think that I understand. Lower subordinate compositions who were linked to the Corps Command at their commands had organs for replenishment and personnel. These were commanders, professional organs, that dealt with these matters, and they were those persons, two, three, five, depending on the command level, with whom, according to the professional level, we communicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir. When the El Mudjahedin Detachment was established, were these professional organs also not established within the El Mudjahedin Detachment so that you can liaise with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The professional organ for replenishment and personnel was never established, and if it was established, I never knew that. And, again, I'm saying that I never had the opportunity to see that. Judging by all that they did, practically, it did not -- not that professional, if you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't, and I would like you to understand what I'm trying to ask. I'm trying to find out, from the point of view of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when they established the El Mudjahedin Detachment, was it not established along the same lines as all other units of the army were established? There must be a commander, there must be a person for replenishment, there must be a person for security, there must be a military police, all those organs that are found in a unit, so that other units must know who to communicate with within this unit? Was that not done for the El Mudjahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, you said, when you're talking about regular units, all the professional organs from the Corps Command down participated in the election of persons at all segments, but in this unit this was never done. We're talking about logistics, security, finances, meaning none such, which indicates an irregular way of organising, if you wish. I simply didn't have access even to be able to say which person would be able to do this professional part or anything else. In the other units that were formed, we did have professionals linked to us. We knew what their abilities were, their options were, and we had a certain kind of influence on them, to a degree, as to how they would need to do this job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand you. Okay, let me put my question differently. You said that in other units, these people participated in elections. Was the El Mudjahedin Detachment not ordered to hold elections of these people and give -- I'm talking now right at the beginning, when it was being established -- and give the names to the superior commands of the various professional organs, or the names of the people holding the various positions in the various professional organs? Was that not done? If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I'm talking about the El Mujahedin, specifically, they did that without any consultations. They did that the way they wanted to. So it would have been logical for the Corps Command organs to have been consulted, to participate, to help, and to help in the selection, in a way, but in their particular case none of this actually was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, I'm getting confused even more. In the one sense, you're saying they hold elections and then they give information. Now you're saying Corps Command organs should have been consulted to participate to help, and that is precisely my question. From the point of view of the army, were the superior commands -- did the superior commands not come and say, "Guys, you are now being subordinated to the army, and this army runs like this: You've got to have a person who holds this position, that position, and that position, and that position, and we want a list of those names," right at the beginning? I would imagine this must have been done to all the other units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This request is not something that I'm aware of, but it was something that was implied. When a command was formed, the command organs, and when I say organs, they participated in the assistance, selection, and so on and so forth. None of this happened, though. I don't know why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have answered me. You're not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I'm also -- I'm also very confused now. I have not understood whether, on the basis of the decree that we saw earlier, whether the volunteers joined other regular units in the army or whether volunteers made up their own units of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was, until then, no case of forming a unit made up of volunteers, which would be composed of volunteers. The volunteers that we talked about before were in the existing units of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Up until then, that's what you said. You meant up until the El Mudjahedin Detachment was set up; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in that specific case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, you considered that the El Mujahid Detachment as a unit made up of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't called that, but in its composition, it was a volunteer unit. But in the formal sense, it was never treated as such anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Volunteers, according to the decree that we just saw, something different, exceptional, outside the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it was formed, this unit, I don't think that it was known, how many men it had, who they were. There was some people who were walking around, so I don't know if it would have made any sense to bring those people under control. There are elements as to whether a person is a volunteer, what does he look like, how many of them are there. I think at the moment it was formed, nobody had any information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, if I can just clarify one part of your last answer. According to the transcript, what it captured was this: "When it was formed, this unit, I don't think that it was known, how many men it had, who they were. There was some people who were walking around, so I don't know if it would have made any sense to bring those people under control." Is that correct, what is recorded in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: My assumption is that in the beginning and when this unit was formed, they didn't have enough elements. And what Her Honour asked about, who were these people, who are they, how many of them are there, this is the reason why this couldn't be defined, because you didn't have the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, I want to go to the issue that His Honour Judge Harhoff wished to raise. During your evidence, you said that on two occasions, you went with a colleague somewhere to try and find out information. Can you please clarify where you and your colleague went to to try and find out information about the El Mudjahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: We went where the Command was officially located in the part of Zenica called "Podbrijezje."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you remember what happened on occasions when you went there to find that information?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: We simply asked to enter the Command, that we had come here with such-and-such an objective, and simply we were refused. There were no persons who were supposed to be, so that we actually ended our job even before we had started it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who did you go there with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was the assistant commander for security who was with me at the time. I don't remember who else was in the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the name of the assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, it was Mr. Adnan Hasanic [as interpreted] who was the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the assistant commander for security, please?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: It was Agan Haseljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And are you able to say approximately what time period it was when you made those two visits?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly, but maybe it was 1995. In any case, judging by this gentleman, when he came, then it could have been 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: When you say "judging by this gentleman," who is the gentleman that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Mr. Agan Haseljic, the one I mentioned earlier when you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to turn to some documents, and I'm just looking at the clock. And rather than getting into a series of documents at this stage, I'm wondering if it might be a good time to take the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We welcome that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm reminded that this is a "D" number, so, please, could I get an exhibit number for this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: First of all, if I could be heard on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On D969?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects on grounds of foundation. This is not a document that has been written by this witness or sent to him. I don't believe there's been a sufficient relationship between this witness and this document shown. I've heard him speculate on why it might have been written, I've heard him read parts of it, but I don't believe a sufficient foundation has been laid for this to be put into evidence. And I do apologise for making this at the last moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has commented on the comment of -- on the content of this document at some length. He has discussed how the document was sent to various units, how -- he talks about his knowledge that the El Mudjahedin Detachment failed to comply, and he spoke about the units, what they did and the ways that they -- that his organ was able to control the unit. So my submission would be that there is a sufficient link to enable the document to be admitted into evidence. It's a document from the 3rd Corps which we know that the -- we know that the witness is a member of the Command of the 3rd Corps, or he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. The document will be admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter D969 is admitted as Exhibit number 1311. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, we do postpone to Monday, in the light of our discussion earlier in the day?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and probably the witness will continue with his testimony the whole day. I think that we will have a witness on Tuesday who will most probably testify on Tuesday and Wednesday. And then most likely there will be no witness for Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Friday, even if you had a witness, I wouldn't be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I think we will only be losing one day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Can I just be reminded? Are we postponing to the afternoon or the morning? There has been some e-mails coming through about the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: Afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, then, Mr. Hubo, we will ask you to come back on Monday afternoon at quarter past 2.00. This is the date to which we postpone the matter. Unfortunately, you'll have to spend the weekend here. I'm sorry about that, but we couldn't finish with you. Okay? The matter is adjourned to quarter past 2.00 on Monday, the 17th, in this courtroom at quarter past 2.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of March, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
